The Yellow-footed antechinus (Antechinus flavipes) is a small dasyurid marsupial endemic to eastern Australia, exhibiting a life history profoundly shaped by its semelparous reproductive strategy. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable ambient temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], researchers have documented a gestation period lasting approximately 31.5 days [tg = approximately 31.5 days], a relatively brief interval that is characteristic of many small-bodied dasyurids. The tiny neonates emerge from the birth canal weighing a mere 0.0164 grams [Wwb = 0.0164 grams], an altricial condition that necessitates an extended period of intense maternal investment. These newborn offspring, often termed pups, immediately attach to a teat within the maternal pouch, where they remain continuously for several weeks. This extreme altriciality at birth is an adaptation linked to the energetic constraints of a small body size and the species' highly synchronized, seasonal breeding cycle.

During their protracted period of dependency within the pouch, the marsupial neonates undergo rapid development, sustained entirely by lactation. At the same thermal regime of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], weaning of the offspring occurs at roughly 90 days since birth [tx = roughly 90 days since birth], marking a critical transition to nutritional independence. By this point, the young have grown considerably and are capable of foraging for invertebrates, shifting from a milk diet to solid food. The maternal investment during the suckling juvenile stage is immense, as the female must provision her growing litter while simultaneously preparing for the post-reproductive physiological collapse that is programmed into the life cycle of all male antechinuses. The successful weaning of a litter is a pivotal event that determines the recruitment of the next generation.

After achieving nutritional independence, the young Yellow-footed antechinus enter a rapid growth and maturation phase. Data from captive populations show that these individuals attain sexual maturity at approximately 320 days since birth [tp = approximately 320 days since birth] when maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This timing aligns with the species' highly synchronized annual breeding season, ensuring that all individuals in a cohort mature simultaneously in preparation for the winter mating period. Puberty onset is marked by testicular development in males and the initiation of ovarian cycling in females. The life history of this species is compressed, with a very brief window between weaning and the onset of reproductive activity, which is a typical feature of mammals in seasonal environments with a short breeding season.

Body size in Antechinus flavipes is sexually dimorphic, with males typically attaining a larger final body size than females. Under optimal conditions, individuals of this species can reach an ultimate wet weight of 45 grams [Wwi = 45 grams], a value that represents the maximum adult body mass. This adult mass is achieved following a period of intense feeding to build the necessary somatic reserves for the energetically costly mating season. The substantial difference in mass between the approximately 0.0164 grams at parturition and the fully grown adult represents a dramatic increase of several orders of magnitude, reflecting a high growth efficiency during the short juvenile phase. The species exhibits no further growth once this adult body mass is attained, as the males typically die after their first breeding season.

The maximum recorded reproductive rate for the Yellow-footed antechinus is a direct consequence of its semelparous life history. Under thermal conditions consistent with this species' active metabolism measured at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], field observations indicate that females typically produce approximately 6 to 7 pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately 6 to 7 pups per litter] and a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year], a stark limitation imposed by the post-mating mortality of all males and the programmed senescence of females that usually occurs shortly after weaning their young. The longevity of these animals is consequently short; the maximum lifespan is approximately 3.9 years [am = approximately 3.9 years] when kept at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], although most wild individuals survive for only a single year due to the programmed die-off of males. This compressed, high-energy reproductive strategy is an evolutionary specialization that prioritizes a single, massive reproductive effort over extended survival.
